title: Thermal Imaging for Early Detection and Identification of Central Venous Catheter Infections
summary:
Many hospital patients, particularly in intensive care or during major surgery, receive a central venous catheter. This is a thin tube inserted into a large vein in the neck, below the collarbone or in the groin, and used to give medication and infusions. Bacteria can settle at the insertion site and cause an infection. Such infections are often recognised late, and it is frequently unclear whether rising inflammation markers in the blood are actually caused by the catheter. Replacing a catheter unnecessarily is demanding and carries its own risks.

Inflamed skin is usually slightly warmer than the healthy skin next to it. A thermal camera can show this temperature difference without contact, without pain and without radiation. In this study, we take thermal images of the insertion site at every routinely scheduled dressing change. After removal, the catheter tip is examined for bacteria in the laboratory, as is done in routine care. We want to find out whether thermal images reliably indicate a catheter infection, and whether they do so earlier than blood tests or visible signs. Participants undergo no additional procedures and face no risks.
conditions: Infection and inflammatory reaction due to other cardiac and vascular devices, implants and grafts

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Indwelling central venous catheter or planned CVC insertion (perioperative or in the intensive care unit)
Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
Refusal to participate
Pre-existing infection at the CVC insertion site
Pre-existing skin disease at the CVC insertion site
